items.stem: Outline how CFCs destroy stratospheric ozone.
items.answer: CFCs are stable and drift into the stratosphere, where UV breaks them down releasing chlorine atoms; Cl + O₃ → ClO + O₂, then ClO + O → Cl + O₂, so chlorine is regenerated and acts as a catalyst destroying many ozone molecules.

items.markingKey: (a) M1 mass ÷ density, A1 2.31 mm. (b) A1 ≈ 65 years. (c) A1 6.0; R1 comparison with formation rate.

The following information comes from a case study.

IPAT comparison (illustrative): Country X - population 300 million, consumption US$60,000 per person, technology 0.25 kg CO₂ per US$; Country Y - population 170 million, consumption US$2,500 per person, technology 0.25 kg CO₂ per US$.

Calculate the total CO₂ impact of each country in million tonnes.
items.markingKey: X: 300 × 10⁶ × 60,000 × 0.25 kg = 4.5 × 10¹² kg = 4,500 Mt; Y: 170 × 10⁶ × 2,500 × 0.25 kg = 1.06 × 10¹¹ kg ≈ 106 Mt. Award [1] per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; quoted data must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem:
Case study extract - Germany's Energiewende: Renewables supplied over half of German electricity in 2023 and the last nuclear plants closed in April 2023.

Using the extract and your own knowledge, explain how this case illustrates political and cultural influences on energy choices.
items.answer: Strong public opposition to nuclear power and climate policy drove a transition that improved long-term security but caused short-term reliance on coal.
items.markingKey: Strong public opposition to nuclear power and climate policy drove a transition that improved long-term security but caused short-term reliance on coal. items.stem:
Resource booklet summary (soy farming in Mato Grosso, Brazil): Brazil is the world's largest soybean producer (about 150 million t), much grown in the Cerrado and southern Amazon for animal feed exports.

Explain what this information reveals about commercial agriculture and its environmental impacts.
items.answer: Large-scale, mechanised monoculture for export drives habitat conversion and pesticide and fertiliser use.
items.markingKey: Large-scale, mechanised monoculture for export drives habitat conversion and pesticide and fertiliser use. Award [1] for each valid point linking the extract to commercial agriculture and its environmental impacts, up to [4]; at least one point must use detail from the extract.

items.stem: With reference to the resource booklet and examples you have studied, evaluate the claim: "The transition to low-carbon energy will be fair to all countries and communities."
items.answer: A just transition is possible but requires deliberate policies on finance, retraining and fair mineral supply chains.
items.markingKey: Strengths / supporting points: cheaper renewables expand energy access; new green jobs. Limitations / counter-points: coal-dependent regions lose jobs; mineral extraction impacts (cobalt, lithium); finance flows mainly to rich countries. Conclusion: A just transition is possible but requires deliberate policies on finance, retraining and fair mineral supply chains. [6]: award [1] for each valid, developed evaluative point (strength or limitation) up to [4], and up to [2] for a balanced, justified conclusion; at least one point must refer explicitly to the case study for full marks.

items.stem: State two differences between biological pest control and chemical pest control.
items.answer: Biological control uses natural enemies (ladybirds, parasitic wasps) to reduce pests with few side effects; chemical control uses pesticides, which act quickly but can harm non-target species, persist and lead to resistance.
items.markingKey: Biological control uses natural enemies (ladybirds, parasitic wasps) to reduce pests with few side effects; chemical control uses pesticides, which act quickly but can harm non-target species, persist and lead to resistance. [1] per valid, explicit comparison up to [3].

items.stem: Outline why international environmental law is difficult to enforce.
items.answer: States are sovereign and agreements depend on voluntary ratification; there is usually no international police or court with compulsory jurisdiction; states may withdraw (USA from Paris in 2017 and 2025); compliance relies on reporting, peer pressure and trade measures.
items.markingKey: States are sovereign and agreements depend on voluntary ratification; there is usually no international police or court with compulsory jurisdiction; states may withdraw (USA from Paris in 2017 and 2025); compliance relies on reporting, peer pressure and trade measures. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: Outline how overgrazing can lead to desertification.
items.answer: Livestock remove vegetation cover and trample soil, compacting it; bare soil is eroded by wind and water, organic matter falls, infiltration declines and rainfall runs off; vegetation cannot re-establish, so degradation spreads.
items.markingKey: Livestock remove vegetation cover and trample soil, compacting it; bare soil is eroded by wind and water, organic matter falls, infiltration declines and rainfall runs off; vegetation cannot re-establish, so degradation spreads. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem:
The following information comes from a case study.

Price of lithium carbonate (approximate, US$ per tonne): 2015 - 6,000; 2018 - 16,000; 2020 - 7,000; late 2022 - 80,000; 2024 - 13,000.

Calculate the percentage increase in price between 2020 and late 2022.
items.markingKey: (80,000 − 7,000)/7,000 × 100 ≈ 1,043%. Award [1] per valid point or correct step, up to [4]; quoted data must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: A 100 g soil sample from a vegetable plot in Nairobi contained sand 30 g, silt 35 g and clay 35 g. Simplified classification: clay ≥ 40%; sand ≥ 85%; silt ≥ 80%; loam if sand 23-52%, silt 28-50% and clay 7-27%; sandy loam if sand 52-85% and clay < 20%; otherwise clay loam. (a) Calculate the percentage composition and classify the soil. (b) Describe how this texture affects its suitability for agriculture. (c) Suggest one way to improve it.
items.answer: (a) sand 30%, silt 35%, clay 35% → clay loam (b) good nutrient retention, moderate drainage; can become waterlogged (c) e.g. add organic matter (compost, manure) to improve structure, water retention and drainage; liming or drainage where needed.
items.markingKey: (a) A1 percentages, A1 clay loam. (b) R1 R1 properties linked to texture. (c) R1 valid improvement.

items.stem: Outline why the composition of waste differs between low- and high-income countries.
items.answer: Low-income countries produce more organic (food) waste as a share; high-income countries produce more paper, plastics, metals and glass from packaged goods and more e-waste.
items.markingKey: Low-income countries produce more organic (food) waste as a share; high-income countries produce more paper, plastics, metals and glass from packaged goods and more e-waste. [1] per valid point, up to [4].

items.stem: With reference to Malham Tarn, UK, field survey, explain in detail the causes and consequences involved in stratified sampling. [7]
items.answer: Students sample limestone grassland and fen using stratified random quadrats in different vegetation zones. Dividing the area into strata ensures each habitat type is represented in the sample. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.

items.stem: With reference to the Great Oxidation Event, explain in detail the causes and consequences involved in the biosphere changing atmospheric composition. [7]
items.answer: About 2.4 billion years ago cyanobacteria released enough oxygen to accumulate in the atmosphere, forming banded iron formations. Photosynthetic organisms transformed the atmosphere, allowing aerobic life and the ozone layer to develop. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.

items.stem: Discuss, from more than one environmental value system, the view that sustainable yield is an effective basis for managing natural resources. [9]
items.answer: Sustainable yield is a sound principle, but it must be applied with precaution and an ecosystem approach to be effective.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: uses natural income without depleting natural capital; quantifiable targets (MSY, allowable cut). Arguments challenging it: population and growth estimates are uncertain; ignores ecosystem interactions and bycatch; political pressure sets quotas above scientific advice. A supported conclusion might be: Sustainable yield is a sound principle, but it must be applied with precaution and an ecosystem approach to be effective. items.stem: "Ozone depletion is a solved environmental problem." Discuss this statement with reference to named examples. [9]
items.answer: Ozone depletion is on the way to being solved, but it requires continued vigilance and enforcement.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: ODS production down over 99%; ozone layer recovering, on track for 2066 in Antarctica. Arguments challenging it: long-lived ODS persist for decades; illegal CFC-11 emissions detected (eastern China, 2010s); HFC substitutes are potent greenhouse gases; climate change affects recovery.
